title: Dat Mäken von Brakel
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, Band 2, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 139. Text from Wikisource (twice proofread against the original). 1857 spelling preserved exactly. This tale is in Low German (Plattdeutsch); the glossary gives the High German equivalent for each dialect form.
about: KHM 139 is a brief Low German comic sketch: a girl visits Saint Anne's chapel to pray for a husband, sings her little rhyme to the saint, and is answered instead by the sexton hiding behind the altar, who calls back that she won't get him. Mishearing the voice for the infant Christ's, she flies into a very earthy rage. It is folk humor at the expense of both piety and the girl, over almost as soon as it starts.

sentences.t: Et gien mal ’n Mäken von Brakel na de sünt Annen Capellen uner de Hinnenborg,
sentences.l: There went once a girl from Brakel to the St Anne’s chapel under the Hinnenborg,
sentences.i: A girl from Brakel once went to the chapel of St Anne below the Hinnenborg,
sentences.n: The whole tale is in Low German (Plattdeutsch), the Westphalian speech of the district it names. Here: Et = es, the impersonal opening “es ging einmal”; gien = ging; mal = einmal, “once” (the adverb, not the noun das Mal); ’n = ein; Mäken = Mädchen; na = nach; uner = unter; sünt = Sankt. Brakel is a small Westphalian town and the Hinnenborg the castle-hill above it, where a chapel of St Anne stood. St Anne, the mother of the Virgin Mary, was the saint an unmarried girl prayed to for a husband — which is the whole premise of what follows.

sentences.t: un weil et gierne ’n Mann heven wulle un ock meinde et wäre süs neimes in de Capellen, sau sank et
sentences.l: and because it would gladly have a husband and also thought there was otherwise nobody in the chapel, so sang it
sentences.i: and because she would dearly have liked a husband, and thought besides that there was nobody else in the chapel, she sang:
sentences.n: sau is so, “so, thus” — not die Sau, a sow; and sank here is sang, the past of singen, not of sinken. gierne = gerne; heven = haben; wulle = wollte; ock = auch; süs = sonst; neimes = niemand. Mann here is a husband, as it often is. wäre is the subjunctive of reported thought — what she supposed, not what the tale asserts. The girl is called et, es, all through the tale, because Mäken (Mädchen) is neuter — English has to say “she.”

sentences.t:
„O hilge sünte Anne,
help mie doch bald tom Manne.
Du kennst ’n ja wull:
he wuhnt var’m Suttmerdore,
hed gele Hore:
du kennst ’n ja wull.“
sentences.l:
“O holy Saint Anne,
do help me soon to a husband.
You know him surely well:
he dwells before the Suttmer gate,
has yellow hair:
you know him surely well.”
sentences.i:
“O holy Saint Anne,
help me to a husband soon.
You know him well enough:
he lives out by the Suttmer gate,
and he has yellow hair —
you know him well enough.”
sentences.n: The prayer is rhymed: Anne with Manne, Dore with Hore, and the last line repeats the third. hilge = heilige; sünte = Sankt; mie = mir; tom = zum; kennst ’n = kennst ihn (this ’n is ihn, where the ’n of “’n Mäken” was ein); wull here is wohl, “well enough, surely,” not wull = wollte as elsewhere; var’m = vor dem (the ’m is dem); Suttmerdore = Suttmertor, a real gate of Brakel; hed = hat; gele = gelbe; Hore = Haare. Naming the man to the saint, with his address and the colour of his hair, is the comedy: she is not asking for a husband, she is asking for that one.

sentences.t: De Köster stand awerst hünner de Altare un höre dat, da rep he mit ’ner gans schrögerigen Stimme „du kriggst ’n nig, du kriggst ’n nig.“
sentences.l: The sexton stood however behind the altar and heard that, then called he with a right dreadful voice “you get him not, you get him not.”
sentences.i: But the sexton was standing behind the altar and heard it, and he called out in a truly dreadful voice: “You shan’t have him, you shan’t have him.”
sentences.n: awerst = aber; hünner = hinter; höre is hörte, the past, not the present; rep = rief; ’ner = einer, the clipped article (not ner = nur); gans = ganz, “quite” (not die Gans, a goose); schrögerigen = schaurigen, ghastly, flesh-creeping; kriggst = kriegst; ’n = ihn. The sexton behind the altar answers the prayer as though he were heaven — the same trick the sexton plays in KHM 68.

sentences.t: Dat Mäken awerst meinde dat Marienkinneken, dat bie de Mudder Anne steiht, hedde üm dat to ropen, da wor et beuse un reip „pepperlepep, dumme Blae, halt de Schnuten un lat de Möhme kühren (die Mutter reden).“
sentences.l: The girl however thought the little Mary-child, that stands by mother Anne, had called that to her; then grew it angry and cried “pepperlepep, stupid brat, hold your snout and let the Möhme talk (the mother talk).”
sentences.i: But the girl thought it was the little Mary-child that stands beside mother Anne who had called it out to her, and she grew angry and cried: “Pepperlepep, you stupid brat, shut your mouth and let your mother do the talking.”
sentences.n: (die Mutter reden) is the Grimms’ own parenthesis, printed in the 1857 text to explain de Möhme kühren to their own readers — not an editorial addition here; the literal line therefore keeps the dialect word and puts their gloss, translated, in the brackets. A Möhme (Muhme) is properly an aunt or kinswoman; the Grimms give it as “the mother.” The Marienkinneken is the little figure of the child Mary standing beside her mother Anne in a carved group of the kind such a chapel held (Anne with Mary and the infant Jesus); the girl takes the voice for the child’s and tells it to leave the talking to its mother. The construction “hedde üm dat to ropen” = hätte ihr das zugerufen, ‘had called that out to her’; üm here is ihm/ihr, where elsewhere üm is um. wor = wurde; beuse = böse; reip = rief; Blae is a Blage, a brat; halt de Schnuten = halt die Schnauze; lat = laß; kühren = reden. pepperlepep is a contemptuous noise, roughly ‘blah blah.’

glossary.gans: Low German: ganz — quite, entirely (not die Gans, the goose)
glossary.halt: halten — hold! (imperative; ‘halt de Schnuten’ = halt die Schnauze)
glossary.höre: Low German: hörte — heard (hören, 3rd sg. past)
glossary.m: ’m — = dem, the (dat.; ‘var’m Suttmerdore’ = vor dem Suttmertor)
glossary.mal: mal — once (adverb, shortened from einmal; ‘et gien mal’ = es ging einmal)
glossary.n: Low German: ’n — ein, a; also = ihn, him (‘du kennst ’n’ = du kennst ihn)
glossary.ner: Low German: ’ner — einer (dat. fem. of ein; ‘mit ’ner Stimme’ = mit einer Stimme)
glossary.sank: Low German: sang — sang (singen, 3rd sg. past; not sank)
glossary.sau: Low German: so — so, thus (not die Sau, the sow)
glossary.wull: Low German: wohl — well enough, surely (‘du kennst ’n ja wull’); elsewhere wull = wollte
glossary.üm: Low German: ihm, ihr — to him, to her (‘hedde üm dat to ropen’ = hätte ihr das zugerufen); elsewhere üm = um
